title: Bad weather
hookLine: Epictetus at sea: once the ship and the day are chosen, the storm isn't his part
tomorrow: a monk said his practice was eating and sleeping. why is that hard?

cards: The weather app shows a wall of red over the weekend, and every plan you had starts to wobble. Epictetus, the Stoic teacher with the lame leg from two weeks back, took his dividing line to sea.
In his Discourses he walks through it. What's my part? To choose the captain, the sailors, the day, the hour.
Then a storm comes. What is that to me now? My part is done, he says.

The decision now belongs to the captain. And if the ship goes down? Then, he says, I do the one thing left: meet it without screaming and without blaming God, knowing that what is born must also pass away.

teach.h: SOME THINGS ARE UP TO US.
teach.b: So, one question: what do you do with what you can't control? Epictetus answers in the first line of his Handbook: some things are up to us, and some are not. Up to us: our judgments, our choices, what we do next.
Not up to us: our bodies, our reputations.
And the weather, plainest of all, isn't ours either. That's the Stoic teaching: peace isn't the storm stopping. It's knowing which part is yours.
A neighbor tradition tells a storm story too. In Mark's Gospel, the disciples are in a boat in a great storm while Jesus sleeps. They wake him: don't you care that we're perishing?
"And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm."

teach.h: THE SEA CALMS, OR THE PASSENGER.
teach.b: Then he asks why they were so afraid. What they share: a storm tests what's inside the boat as much as the boat.
The honest difference: in Mark, Jesus stills the sea, and Christians read it as showing who he is. Epictetus never expects the sea to calm. Only the passenger changes.

how: Readers of Epictetus sort what is up to them from what isn't, and practice meeting what isn't, like the weather, with calm judgment. Christians read Mark's storm story as showing who Jesus is.

o: a forecast to check before you head outside
a storm that isn't yours to control, only to meet
a sign that your plans were a bad idea

games.q: two storms at sea: tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says that once the ship and day are chosen, the storm isn't your part

games.q: your sister's outdoor wedding gets rained on, and she's in tears in the tent. what fits Epictetus?
o: the rain was never hers to control; what's hers now is how she meets the day.
tell her it's her fault: she should have picked an indoor venue.
find who's to blame: Epictetus says every bad outcome needs a culprit.
games.why: some things are up to us and some are not. the weather is the plainest of the second kind; meeting it is the first.

practice: If there's a window near you, look at the sky as it is, whatever it's doing. If not, listen for the weather: wind, rain, traffic on wet roads, or the quiet.
Let it be exactly what it is, not up to you, and notice the part that is: how you're meeting it.

wordCard.voice: Bad weather: Epictetus's plainest lesson in what isn't up to us. The storm belongs to the sky; how you meet it is yours.

orig.note: Greek: up to us. Epictetus's Handbook opens by sorting what is up to us from what isn't.

carryVoice: Carry this: the weather is the sky's part, and the passenger's calm is yours. That's eight of the fourteen.
